findings: Rate limiter buckets by `req.ip` (`const key = req.ip`) instead of by API key, directly contradicting the docs' claim that "Each API key is limited to 100 requests per minute" — no API key/token is referenced anywhere in checkLimit. On a shared-office network, all users/API keys behind the same NAT'd public IP share one bucket, so the effective per-key budget becomes 100/N (N = concurrent users on that IP) instead of 100, exactly matching the reported symptom of being rate-limited far more easily than documented.

Because bucketing is IP-based rather than key-based, one customer's traffic on a shared office IP can exhaust the shared bucket and cause HTTP 429s for other, unrelated API keys/tenants on that same IP even though those tenants are individually nowhere near 100 requests — a noisy-neighbor denial-of-service enabled directly by the keying bug.

There is no time-window logic at all: buckets is a plain Map that is only ever incremented, with no timestamps, no per-minute reset, and no expiry/eviction of entries. This turns the documented "100 requests per minute" (a recurring per-minute allowance) into a cumulative lifetime cap per key/IP for the life of the process — once 100 requests have ever been sent, that IP is permanently blocked until the server restarts, compounding the shared-IP problem rather than resetting each minute as documented.

The docs promise a `Retry-After` header telling the client when to retry, but checkLimit has no timestamp/window-start data to compute such a value from (it returns only `{limited: true}`); with no per-minute window tracked, there is no correct value that could be produced for Retry-After, so the documented retry guidance cannot actually be honored by this implementation.

buckets never removes or expires keys, so it grows without bound as new IPs make requests, which combined with the missing time-window reset also creates an unbounded in-memory growth (memory leak) risk over the process lifetime.
